name: D-8 Corporate Investment (Foreign-Invested Enterprise Representative)

requirements.blocker_text: Requires a minimum investment of KRW 100 million (roughly USD 70,000-75,000) under the Foreign Investment Promotion Act, remitted from abroad into the Korean company's account -- funds already held in a domestic Korean account do not qualify. If two foreigners co-invest, each must separately contribute at least KRW 100 million; a combined KRW 100 million split between two applicants does not qualify either of them.
requirements.fix_path: Remit at least KRW 100 million in qualifying foreign-investment funds into the Korean corporation's account.

requirements.blocker_text: The investor must hold at least 10% of the invested company's voting shares and actively participate in management as an executive.
requirements.fix_path: Confirm shareholding structure meets the 10% minimum and management role is documented.

evidence_required.document: Bank remittance records showing the qualifying investment amount arriving from abroad
Business premises appropriate to the company's operations (a shared-office address alone is often insufficient)

outcome.duration_length: 1-3 years, renewed subject to demonstrating actual business operations (revenue, tax filings) rather than dormant capital

sources.title: HiKorea -- Korea Immigration Service's official portal for visa categories, ARC, and stay procedures

notes: The KRW 100 million (roughly USD 70,000) minimum is notably low by the standards of comparable investor-residency products in this dataset -- several independent sources note this explicitly, observing that even countries with lower GNI than Korea's often require substantially more for an equivalent investor route, and one Korean-language source frames D-8 as functioning as a de facto family-immigration product at this price point (spouse and children can accompany via F-3 dependent status) precisely because the bar is so low relative to Korea's income level. Distinguished from kr_d8_4_oasis_startup, which shares the D-8 visa-code family but requires zero capital in exchange for a 60+ point technology/credential assessment -- the two are structurally different qualifying paths, not scaled versions of the same test, correctly modeled as separate route files rather than requirement_groups within one route given how differently their evidence and blocker logic work. Renewal scrutiny has tightened as of 2026 per multiple sources: consular and immigration officers now focus specifically on whether the invested capital shows genuine business activity (revenue, tax filings, operational records) rather than remaining untouched in the company account, a meaningful practical difference between initial approval and renewal that's worth surfacing on the route detail page. Investment amount is per-investor, not per-company: two co-founders cannot pool a single KRW 100 million contribution to both qualify -- each needs their own qualifying KRW 100 million, a specific and easy-to-miss structural trap flagged repeatedly across independent sources.
